sources.title: Joseph Zada Tells Elle Fanning How the Odds Became Ever In His Favor
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada, in conversation with Elle Fanning; Interview Magazine, September 2026 issue (no writer byline; conversation transcript)
sources.date: 2026-08-10 (published); conversation slugged 'FRIDAY 2 PM JUN 12, 2026 NEW YORK CITY'
sources.locator: Full transcript. Key exchanges: audition/callback sequence ('I flew back to Australia from New Zealand'); reaction to the casting call ('I just started swearing'); name-change explanation ('My original name is Cumpston'); Hunger Games team ('a perfectly curated team. It's also a family'); family/origins ('it only properly appealed to me at about 15'); 'Who are you when you're not a character, Joe?'
sources.excerpt: ZADA: ... Because I was shooting, I told them, 'I'll have it to you in three weeks,' because I had a plan to shoot the scenes properly and edit them. It's a crazy audition and I really went all out. / FANNING: Did Florence [Pugh] help you with the audition? / ZADA: No, she didn't. Actually, I flew back to Australia from New Zealand just so I could work with my older brother. He helped me, and so did my dad and a couple of friends. ... I got back to Sydney and woke to a 7 a.m. call from my entire team, so I more or less knew immediately. I just started swearing, like, 'Now I have to do this and it's going to be really hard.' / FANNING: [Laughs] You were more scared after finding out? / ZADA: Yes.
sources.context: Longest and most recent primary source, and the only one published after he finished shooting Sunrise on the Reaping. A peer-to-peer celebrity conversation for a fashion title, so it is promotional and friendly, but it is unusually specific about process and chronology. Opened in full via a reader proxy after the publisher returned HTTP 403 to direct requests; the proxy returned the complete article body with byline, publication timestamp and the dateline block. Fanning is a Sunrise on the Reaping co-star, not a neutral interviewer. Draft stage (2026-09-13) reopened the transcript via reader proxy and verified every quotation used. Two corrections to the research record: the 'Yes' after 'You were more scared after finding out?' continues 'Then the announcement came out a day after'; and the name-change passage is two separate replies, not one. The person who asked him not to watch the 1955 East of Eden is referred to only as 'she', and the voice passage does not mention coaches. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened this source in full via reader proxy. Verified additionally: his heritage answer ('My grandmother's Australian Indigenous and also Afghan. The name comes from my great-grandfather, who was an Afghan cameleer. Our family built the first mosque in Australia, so it's got great history, that name. I felt a weird spiritual connection to it'); the East of Eden callback exchange ('I was thinking maybe after I got the role,' then 'Promise me you won't watch the film') and his aside 'But also, I'm in the last two episodes'; the coaches line, which does exist and concerns the accent ('I worked with quite a few coaches, but I more or less had to let go at some point and try not to focus on the accent'), correcting the draft-stage note; the bucket-list exchange ('I love the actors I love, but I'm shit scared of working with them' / 'I don't know how excited I'd be as opposed to deathly nervous'); Pugh ('She's scary... It was very daunting, but she's so friendly and makes everyone feel so comfortable'); 'He's six years older than me' about the older brother; and the plan to live in L.A., New York or London despite his mother's preference. The intro identifies Cal Trask as 'the role that made James Dean a legend'.

sources.title: Sharing the Ride (Joseph Zada in conversation with Esther McGregor)
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada, interviewed by Esther McGregor; Behind The Blinds, edited by Pedro Vasconcelos, posted by Martin Onufrowicz
sources.locator: Full transcript. Key passages: opening location answer (Berlin, family flown in); 'What surprised you about being on set?'; East of Eden answer ('it was the cast and the filmmakers'); Hunger Games nerves ('phenomenally nervous'); directing ambition ('before I'm 30').
sources.excerpt: JZ: I'm here with my older brother, and I just brought over my dad and my little brother. We're going to Portugal tomorrow for the weekend, which will be really fun, just a little boys' trip right before I jump into the deep end with this. ... At the start, I was so nervous. I worked myself into a state of so much anxiety and put too much pressure on myself. But by the time I got into the flow, I found my footing. ... There's definitely a lot of pressure, but funny enough, it wasn't so much the legacy of the story that scared me; it was the cast and the filmmakers. These are people I really admire. I was just afraid of how they would perceive me. ... I feel both of us get lonely; we need someone around.
sources.context: Conducted while Zada was in Berlin in prep for Sunrise on the Reaping, before that shoot began. The interviewer is his We Were Liars co-star and close friend, which makes the register loose and self-disclosing but removes any adversarial check. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened the full text via reader proxy and corrected two draft-stage errors: the David Morse passage IS present ('I was very excited to work with David [Morse], especially because my dad spoke so highly of him... Dad and I sat down before I went over and watched all of David's films together'), and so is the co-writing plan ('I've already started writing'; 'me and Hal, my older brother, we're writing a movie together right now'). The loneliness line answers McGregor's question 'What's your favourite memory of the two of us?' and introduces nightly hangouts on a Halifax balcony. He also says 'The press side of things, people make it sound stressful, but I've enjoyed it.'

sources.title: “It's weird to be a part of something that you've been such a massive fan of” – Mckenna Grace in conversation with Joseph Zada
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace; HERO / HEROINE 24, introduced by Alex James Taylor
sources.locator: Full transcript. Key passages: 'being forced to spend family time'; Grace on his note-keeping; 'Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable'; headphones; career sequence ('As I turned eighteen'); what he wants next.
sources.excerpt: JZ: And being forced to spend family time so I wasn't chilling in my own head and going crazy by myself. ... MG: ... you kept the most intricate notes. Then you and I sat and watched all of The Hunger Games movies and took notes. ... JZ: Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable. ... JZ: I can't really do the emotional scenes without headphones. I feel like I always walk around in some crazy little cloud with my headphones on. ... JZ: As I turned eighteen, I got the lead role in Invisible Boys, and then I jumped straight to We Were Liars, and then straight to East of Eden, and then straight to Hunger Games.
sources.context: Two-way conversation with his Sunrise on the Reaping co-star, recorded after that shoot wrapped. Valuable for two reasons: Grace supplies third-party observation of his working method (the 'most intricate notes'), and Zada volunteers the line about needing enforced company to stay out of his own head, which is the single most self-aware statement in the record. Promotional context still applies; both parties are praising each other throughout. Reopened 2026-09-13. Verified quotations used. The research record's co-writing project with his brother and the dinners with Grace's mother were not found in the retrieved text and are not used. Contains 'Our first night in Spain, I'd just turned twenty', consistent with a 2005 birth. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened this source in full via reader proxy. Context now recorded: the 'family time' line follows Grace saying 'when you were too tired from stunts and everything to come out or hang out, I would make you come and have dinner with my mom every night' and Zada replying 'It's so lovely to have you and your mom and Iona's [Bell] mom'; the family is Grace's, formed on location in Spain. 'Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable' follows Grace praising the young IT: Welcome to Derry cast ('Those kids are so good'), and he goes on to joke about a twelve-year-old 'acting you off the table'. Also verified: 'All the sound people hate the idea of you having something actually playing... I begged them to let me play it because I needed it to give me that energy' (an early Invisible Boys scene), and 'I kind of want to wait for a little bit, and I want the right thing to come up next'. The co-writing project is in S02, not here.

sources.title: Joseph Zada | Salt, Swagger, and Reckless Abandon
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada, profiled by Maddy Brown; Flaunt Magazine
sources.date: unknown exact day (page metadata reports 2025-09-10, but the text treats the We Were Liars release day as past and Sunrise filming as not yet begun, and the image asset IDs encode late June 2025; placed around the June 2025 release; accessed 2026-09-13)
sources.locator: Full profile. Key passages: 'really happy, actually'; footballer/Arsenal and the age-15 origin; the London bus advertisement; 'I don't want anyone to know anything about me'; 'still learning' / 'stay in my own lane'; 'go toe to toe with anyone now'.
sources.excerpt: “I've said this a lot, but I do just feel like I'm still learning. I think it's a lot of pressure, but I'm just constantly reminding myself that I'm still learning and not to be afraid of whether it's good or not,” Zada says. “Unfortunately, I'm just learning on a pretty big stage where there is a lot of noise, but I try to block it all out and stay in my own lane.” ... “I'm kind of in a weird place right now. I don't want anyone to know anything about me. But now I'm in these situations where I do have to talk about it,” acknowledges Zada. ... “I'm feeling a bit more confident now, and also because I just learned that these people are actually normal people and they're doing the same thing that I'm doing. I have it in me to go toe to toe with Florence [Pugh], I think. I feel like I can go toe to toe with anyone now.”
sources.context: A written profile rather than a Q&A, so the writer's framing is doing work: Brown repeatedly characterises Zada as 'zen', 'chill' and 'good-natured', which is an observer's read that partly contradicts the anxiety he reports elsewhere. That tension is useful counterevidence and is treated as such. The piece carries no publication date, which limits how precisely it can be placed; only the fact that We Were Liars had been released is anchored by its own text. Reopened 2026-09-13; quotations used were verified. The Arsenal detail is the writer's paraphrase, not a quotation. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened this source in full via reader proxy. The writer names the brother he helped as Hal: 'It was only after helping his older brother Hal, who is also an actor, with self-tapes that a love of acting was sparked in him.' The 'uncommonly zen mentality' line follows his own joking self-description, 'extremely talented, extremely chill, and extremely humble', which the writer says is 'all said in jest'.

sources.title: Out of the Darkness: ‘Invisible Boys' Shines Light on Queer Stories
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada, reported by Julie Hosking from the Invisible Boys set in Perth; Variety Australia/New Zealand
sources.locator: Opening section, paragraphs 1–7, covering Zada before the piece moves to Calafiore and the wider production.
sources.excerpt: “I had a lot of stuff going on when I was younger and some schools just don't know how to handle that, and I ended up being kicked out,” he says. “I was going to an all-boys school and there was a bit of a stigma around acting. I just thought it was a very vulnerable place to be.” ... Sporting Charlie's spectacular shock of aquamarine hair, Zada is remarkably upbeat for someone who has spent much of the past week in tears. “I had crying, emotional scenes almost every day last week, and I don't tend to wear my emotions on my sleeve like Charlie does,” he says. “But I think it was very good for me coming into this character and this role – it's taught me to be vulnerable. I have more access to my emotions, and I think that's been a very big gift.”
sources.context: Trade reporter Julie Hosking's set visit to Invisible Boys in Perth ('The debutante ball scene is being filmed in an old hall before production moves north to Geraldton'), published February 13, 2025, the premiere day. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened the full text. The visit date is not printed; Stan's March 12, 2024 release (S23) says the series was then filming in Perth and Geraldton, with production stills dated January to February 2024, so the interview was given in early 2024, when he was 18 and unknown, not in February 2025. The piece also says he 'was still at school when he learned he would play' Charlie, 'a punk rocker who is outed on social media after an encounter with a married man'. Load-bearing for the first school-exit account ('I ended up being kicked out') and for Hosking's observation that he was 'remarkably upbeat' after a week of crying scenes.

Because castmates were present, the answers are shaped for a shared audience.

sources.title: ‘We Were Liars' Star Joseph Zada On Playing Haymitch Abernathy In ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping': “I'm So Ridiculously Nervous”
sources.speaker: Joseph Zada and E. Lockhart, reported by Dessi Gomez; Deadline
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2–5, including Lockhart's casting testimony.
sources.excerpt: “I've seen scripts. I can't say anything,” Zada told Deadline during the press day for We Were Liars. “I've read the book twice already.” ... “I'm a very, very, very big fan of everything to do with it and the whole cast and everyone involved,” Zada added. “I'm so ridiculously nervous.” ... “We had seen many, many, many handsome guys, and we had seen many, many, many very funny guys... And [Joseph] was all those things, but he also really communicated the pain underneath Johnny's humor and also underneath Johnny's bad behavior,” Lockhart told Deadline. “He was showing us a kid who was complicated, hurting, relatable as well as snarky and badly behaved.”
sources.context: Trade report from the We Were Liars press day. Supplies named professional testimony from E. Lockhart, the novel's author and an executive producer, who was in the casting room. Lockhart is describing his audition performance, not his character offscreen, so it is evidence about his craft and the impression he made on decision-makers rather than about his motives.

sources.title: Joseph Zada Was Up Against “Really Big” Names for Haymitch Role in ‘Sunrise on the Reaping'
sources.speaker: Emily Alyn Lind, quoted by Lexy Perez; The Hollywood Reporter, relaying an interview Lind gave to People
sources.locator: Paragraphs 2–6.
sources.excerpt: “So, I was FaceTiming him because he was like, ‘I'm in L.A.' And I'm like, ‘What are you doing in L.A., loser? Let's hang out,'” Emily Alyn Lind said. “And I FaceTime him and he is at this hotel and he's being Joe. And he's like, ‘Yeah, I'm out here. You can't tell anyone but it's down to me and a couple [other] people for this Hunger Games thing.'” ... “And he's naming names that are really big that he's up against.” ... “I'm like, ‘You'll get it, because you're you.'” “He just gets what he wants,” she said of Zada. “He is going to be one of these guys.”
sources.context: The most useful counterevidence in the packet and the reason it is recorded prominently. Lind is a We Were Liars co-star describing a private FaceTime call during the Haymitch callbacks, not a press appearance. Her characterisation, 'He just gets what he wants', attributes appetite and agency rather than anxiety, and she reports him tracking his competition by name. Two caveats: THR is relaying a People interview rather than reporting it first-hand, so this is one remove from the original, and Lind is speaking affectionately about a friend. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened this source in full via reader proxy. Sequence clarified: the private FaceTime supplies what he did (shortlist told in confidence, naming big competitors). 'He just gets what he wants' and 'He is going to be one of these guys' are Lind's characterisation to People, following her recollection 'I'm like, "You'll get it, because you're you."'

sources.title: Joseph Zada
sources.speaker: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: Infobox; 'Early and personal life'; 'Career' sections.
sources.excerpt: Joseph Cumpston (born July 21, 2005), known professionally as Joseph Zada, is an Australian actor. ... His father, Jeremy Cumpston, is a director, actor, and doctor. His mother, Jessica Brentnall is a film producer. He has four siblings, including Hal Cumpston. ... Zada dropped out of high school in 2023 to pursue acting, telling GQ Australia: “My attendance was too low. They said, ‘If you do that audition, you're not coming back.' So I dropped out to do an audition.” ... In December 2025, Zada was named Breakthrough Actor of the Year by GQ Australia magazine.
sources.context: Tertiary compilation used for the timeline, the legal name and birth date, and as a pointer to citations. It is the only readable route to the GQ Australia quotation, since GQ's own site is hard-blocked (S18). Two internal tensions are noted rather than resolved: Wikipedia describes Hal Cumpston as a half-brother while Zada and profile writers say 'older brother' without qualification, and Wikipedia places the Afghan-Aboriginal line at the paternal great-grandmother while Zada attributes the Zada name to his grandmother and his great-grandfather (S01). Not treated as independent corroboration of anything. Reopened 2026-09-13. Its citations attribute the school-exit quotation to Karen Leong, "'I'm trying to learn and bring something new': Joseph Zada's ascent begins", GQ Australia, 17 December 2025, and the award to Karen Leong, 'Joseph Zada is GQ's Breakthrough Actor of the Year for 2025', GQ Australia, 24 March 2026 (gq.com.au/men-of-the-year/...). The award therefore should not be dated December 2025. Edit stage (2026-09-13) reopened the raw wikitext: it records Afghan-Aboriginal heritage through the paternal great-grandmother and a Barkandji link, which is compatible with Zada's own account that his grandmother is Indigenous and Afghan and the surname came from her cameleer father; the draft's framing of a conflict was withdrawn. It dates the Haymitch casting announcement to April 2025 (Deadline, April 23, 2025).

claims.claim: Joseph Zada is an Australian actor born in 2005.
claims.passage: an Australian actor born in 2005
claims.inference: The year is consistent across ages given in dated interviews (20 in Polyester on 2025-06-18; 21 in Interview on 2026-08-10) and with his own remark to Mckenna Grace that he had 'just turned twenty' on the first night in Spain during the summer 2025 shoot (S03). The July 21 day and month come from Wikipedia alone, so the draft prints only the year and no birth_date metadata.
claims.alternative: If no primary source for the day emerges, write 'born in 2005' and give his age with the date of the source. Never convert the birth date to January 1, and do not print July 21 as established fact on a single tertiary source.

claims.claim: He works professionally as Joseph Zada, having taken his grandmother's surname in place of his legal surname, Cumpston, while on his last callback before a career-defining job.
claims.passage: "My original name is Cumpston, which my older brother still goes by," he told Fanning. Zada is his grandmother's surname. "When I was starting out, about to go for my big break, I was on my last callback and I'd been thinking about changing my name."
claims.inference: Reopened 2026-09-13. In the transcript these are two separate replies: 'My original name is Cumpston, which my older brother still goes by.' then, after a Fanning interjection, 'Yes. But my grandmother's last name is Zada. When I was starting out...'. The draft quotes them as two quotations with a paraphrase between, not as one joined quotation. The timing is his own framing.
claims.alternative: A name change at the start of a career is also ordinary industry practice, especially where a sibling already works under the original surname and a distinct credit is useful. His stated reason and the practical reason are not mutually exclusive.

claims.claim: He says his grandmother is Australian Indigenous and Afghan, that the Zada name comes from his Afghan cameleer great-grandfather, and that his family built the first mosque in Australia.
claims.passage: He went on: "My grandmother's Australian Indigenous and also Afghan. The name comes from my great-grandfather, who was an Afghan cameleer." He says "our family built the first mosque in Australia,"
claims.inference: Direct quotations verified in S01 on 2026-09-13. Wikipedia (S15) independently records Afghan-Aboriginal heritage and a Barkandji link, which fits his account; there is no contradiction to report. The mosque line is attributed to him as family history.
claims.alternative: Several Australian sites make competing first-mosque claims, so the article presents it only as what he says, without adding doubt about his heritage.

claims.claim: His father, Jeremy Cumpston, is a director, actor and doctor, and his mother, Jessica Brentnall, is a film producer.
claims.passage: His father, Jeremy Cumpston, has worked as a director, actor and doctor, and his mother, Jessica Brentnall, as a film producer
claims.inference: Wikipedia (S15) gives both occupations; Zada himself says 'My mom is a producer too, or was a producer' (S01), so the article uses career descriptions rather than present-tense status. Acting was the family's ordinary world.
claims.alternative: An industry upbringing is a strong non-psychological explanation for much of his trajectory, including his access, his comfort with sets and his early credits. Any account of his drive has to survive the fact that this path was the path of least resistance in his household.

claims.claim: He says acting only properly appealed to him at about 15, when he began helping his older brother with auditions.
claims.passage: "It only properly appealed to me at about 15, when I started helping my older brother with auditions when he'd come back from America," he told Fanning.
claims.inference: Verified in S01; Flaunt (S04) independently tells the same origin and names the brother as Hal. The origin is relational: he found acting as his brother's reader.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia records a first credit in 2019's Bilched, when he was 13 or 14, in a film directed by his father and starring Hal. So he was acting on camera before the age-15 awakening he describes. The two are reconcilable if the early role was family participation rather than pursuit, but the 'started at 15' framing should not be printed as though he had no prior screen work.

claims.claim: He and Hal prepared auditions together for up to eight hours at a stretch, running scenes a hundred different ways.
claims.passage: "We'd work up to eight hours on auditions," he said. "We'd drive each other to the proper limits of a scene and try to do it 100 different ways just for fun."
claims.inference: Verified in S01. The auditions were his brother's (C05), so the article treats the sessions as the formative habit of preparing with a partner, not as an instance of family gathering before his own threshold.
claims.alternative: 'Eight hours' and '100 different ways' are conversational magnitudes, not measurements, and the anecdote is told warmly to a peer. Treat as characterisation of a habit, not as a logged practice.

claims.claim: He left school in 2023, in circumstances he has described in two ways that do not match: to Variety on the Invisible Boys set he said he 'ended up being kicked out' of an all-boys school after 'a lot of stuff going on when I was younger'; to GQ Australia he said his attendance was too low and that he chose to drop out when told an audition would end his enrolment.
claims.passage: Wikipedia relays a different version from a December 2025 GQ Australia interview: "My attendance was too low. They said, 'If you do that audition, you're not coming back.' So I dropped out to do an audition."
claims.inference: S06 was reopened 2026-09-13 and the 'kicked out' wording matches. The GQ quotation still reaches the record only through Wikipedia, which cites it to Karen Leong, GQ Australia, 17 December 2025. The two accounts assign agency in opposite directions; the draft quotes both, says they differ, and builds no psychological claim on either.
claims.alternative: Both versions are quoted; neither is used as evidence for any type, including Type 3. The GQ original remains unopened (S18).
claims.review_trigger: If GQ Australia's December 2025 interview becomes readable, or if he gives a third account of leaving school, reconcile this claim and correct any passage that leans on one version.

claims.claim: He also said the all-boys school carried 'a bit of a stigma around acting' and that he 'just thought it was a very vulnerable place to be'.
claims.passage: "I was going to an all-boys school and there was a bit of a stigma around acting. I just thought it was a very vulnerable place to be."
claims.inference: Direct quotation, given on the Perth set during the early-2024 Invisible Boys shoot (S23), when he was 18 and unknown, and published February 13, 2025. Locates the difficulty in exposure to peer judgment.
claims.alternative: Stigma around drama at an all-boys school is a common and largely environmental fact, so this evidences a real constraint he faced more than a disposition he brought. It should not be used as a childhood-wound explanation for anything.

claims.claim: He got the lead in Invisible Boys as he turned 18 and then worked almost continuously through We Were Liars, East of Eden and Sunrise on the Reaping with roughly two months off between jobs.
claims.passage: "As I turned eighteen, I got the lead role in _Invisible Boys_, and then I jumped straight to _We Were Liars_, and then straight to _East of Eden_, and then straight to _Hunger Games_,"
claims.inference: His own sequencing in S03 ('With like two months off in between'), corroborated by the East of Eden window in S16.
claims.alternative: A run of back-to-back jobs at 18 to 20 reflects being cast repeatedly as much as it reflects appetite. Availability and momentum explain a great deal; do not read the schedule alone as evidence of a motive.

claims.claim: Asked for one improvised scene for the Haymitch audition while shooting East of Eden, he asked for three weeks so he could shoot and edit the scenes properly, and flew from New Zealand back to Australia to prepare with his older brother, his father and friends.
claims.passage: "I flew back to Australia from New Zealand just so I could work with my older brother. He helped me, and so did my dad and a couple of friends."
claims.inference: Verified in S01, where it answers Fanning's 'Did Florence [Pugh] help you with the audition?'. The article now states the skill explanation first (a director father and actor brother were the best crew for a properly shot tape) and treats the relational phrasing ('just so I could work with my older brother') as consistent with, not proof of, the Six reading. Geography consistent with S16.
claims.alternative: Skill and resources explain the choice of collaborators; the trip may also have fit a schedule break. The article says both.

claims.claim: Asked by Elle Fanning whether he was more scared after learning he had won the role of Haymitch, he said yes.
claims.passage: Fanning laughed and asked, "You were more scared after finding out?" He said "Yes," and moved straight on: "Then the announcement came out a day after, so everyone found out at the same time as me. It was pretty full-on."
claims.inference: Verified verbatim. 'More scared' is Fanning's laughing paraphrase, which he accepted with 'Yes' before moving to logistics. The article treats this as a supporting datum, not a discriminator, and places the same-morning celebration with his sister (C41) beside it.
claims.alternative: Told more than a year later to a co-star in a promotional conversation for a franchise whose premise makes winning dangerous; a big obligation could alarm a Nine or a Three too. Both limits are stated in the article.

claims.claim: He says what scared him about East of Eden was not the material's legacy but the people: 'it was the cast and the filmmakers. These are people I really admire. I was just afraid of how they would perceive me.'
claims.passage: "funny enough, it wasn't so much the legacy of the story that scared me; it was the cast and the filmmakers. These are people I really admire. I was just afraid of how they would perceive me."
claims.inference: He passed over the legacy answer McGregor's question offered. The article now treats this quote as neutral between Six and Three, and as ordinary newcomer fear, and locates the discriminator in what settles the fear (C14, C19, C66, C67, C94).
claims.alternative: Deferring to a distinguished cast is the expected humility register for a newcomer, and it was said to a close friend. He immediately adds 'But I got over that quickly' (C61), which the draft quotes, so the fear is presented as passing.

claims.claim: Before Sunrise on the Reaping began, he said that as on every other project, once he stepped on set and met everyone he would be fine.
claims.passage: he said he was "phenomenally nervous," then offered his usual fix: "like every other project I've done, I think once I step on set and meet everyone, I'll be fine."
claims.inference: Present-tense statement from Berlin prep, framed as habitual ('like every other project'). A remedy statement: meeting the people is what he expects to settle nerves.
claims.alternative: The S12 quotation reaches this packet only through CinemaBlend's relay of a Swooon interview that could not be opened (S19), so its exact wording is unverified against the original. Treat the wording as reported rather than confirmed.

claims.claim: Of nights in Halifax during We Were Liars, he told Esther McGregor that both of them get lonely and need someone around.
claims.passage: "I feel both of us get lonely; we need someone around."
claims.inference: Verified in S02, where it is the first line of his answer to 'What's your favourite memory of the two of us?'. The article frames it that way. Paired with C68 (HERO, published 2026-03-23), about eight and a half months after S02 (2025-07-09), not fourteen months.
claims.alternative: Loneliness abroad is ordinary at his age and this is a friendship memory; it supports only the modest claim that company steadies him.

claims.claim: He brings family to the threshold of big jobs: he flew his father and younger brother to Berlin and travelled with his older brother immediately before Sunrise on the Reaping began, calling it 'a little boys' trip right before I jump into the deep end'.
claims.passage: "I'm here with my older brother, and I just brought over my dad and my little brother. We're going to Portugal tomorrow for the weekend, which will be really fun, just a little boys' trip right before I jump into the deep end with this."
claims.inference: Present tense, from Berlin. With the flight home for the Haymitch tape (C11) it gives two clear instances of family around his own threshold; the teenage sessions (C06) are treated as habit, not a third instance.
claims.alternative: Flying family to a European job is also simply what someone does with a first significant pay cheque, and 'the deep end' is a light phrase, not a confession. The pattern is the evidence; any single instance is ordinary.

claims.claim: He told People that Glenn Close made it clear she was always there for him.
claims.passage: "It means so much to have someone of such stature support you, and Glenn in particular made it clear she was always there for me."
claims.inference: What he singles out is Close's reliability ('made it clear she was always there for me'), which the article uses as reliability language rather than approval language.
claims.alternative: Praising a celebrated co-star warmly is obligatory in a People interview and tells you little on its own. Read via a Yahoo syndication of People rather than People directly, so it is a readable copy, not independent corroboration.

claims.claim: In mid-2025 he told Polyester he did not want to set a method in stone because he was new to the game.
claims.passage: "I have a lot of ways of preparing but I'm also very new to the game, so I don't want to set anything in stone right now,"
claims.inference: Three separate publications within about a month of each other in mid-2025, each carrying the same pre-emptive hedge attached to a different subject: process, performance and future ambition. The hedge travels with him rather than belonging to one topic.
claims.alternative: This is also exactly what a well-advised 19-year-old says in his first press cycle, and 'I'm still learning' is the safest available sentence for a newcomer cast opposite Oscar winners. The confound is serious and the three sources are not independent of the same publicity window.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck after the Sunrise on the Reaping and East of Eden releases. If he speaks with settled authority about his own method once the work is public, this hedging was a phase of career position rather than a disposition, and the claim should be requalified.

claims.claim: At his first East of Eden callback he said he planned to watch the 1955 film after getting the role, was asked to promise not to, agreed, and waited about eight months.
claims.passage: "I said, 'Yeah, sure. I guess I won't watch it.'" He waited about eight months.
claims.inference: Verified in S01. An instruction he followed after stating a different plan, with no approval afterward; the article no longer calls it his own method or part of an avoid-then-approval sequence.
claims.alternative: Avoiding a previous performance of the same role is standard craft advice, so the compliance is not distinctive. 'whose lead role James Dean played in the 1955 film' rests on S01 ('an incredible, incredible performance from James Dean') and S16's note of the 1955 adaptation.

claims.claim: He says he does not want to be known: 'I'm kind of in a weird place right now. I don't want anyone to know anything about me. But now I'm in these situations where I do have to talk about it.'
claims.passage: "I'm kind of in a weird place right now. I don't want anyone to know anything about me. But now I'm in these situations where I do have to talk about it."
claims.inference: He supplies the reason in the same passage ('But now I'm in these situations where I do have to talk about it'), and most later openness is promotional. The article acknowledges both and leaves open only how much he volunteers beyond the job.
claims.alternative: He also told McGregor he has enjoyed press (S02). The remaining tension is modest and stated as such.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck after the November 2026 release. If his press posture changes markedly in either direction, this claim needs requalifying.

claims.claim: After East of Eden he said his confidence had risen, in comparative terms: 'I have it in me to go toe to toe with Florence [Pugh], I think. I feel like I can go toe to toe with anyone now.'
claims.passage: "I just learned that these people are actually normal people and they're doing the same thing that I'm doing. I have it in me to go toe to toe with Florence [Pugh], I think. I feel like I can go toe to toe with anyone now."
claims.inference: Counterevidence to a purely anxious reading, and recorded as such. Note the mechanism he gives for the change, which is not self-belief but reclassification of the others: 'I just learned that these people are actually normal people and they're doing the same thing that I'm doing.' The threat was demoted before the confidence arrived.
claims.alternative: It reads equally well as straightforward emerging self-assurance in a talented 19-year-old who has just held his own opposite an Oscar winner. The 'I think' hedge inside the first sentence is doing visible work, but a reading that treats every hedge as significant is unfalsifiable and must be resisted.

claims.claim: Emily Alyn Lind told People, 'He just gets what he wants' and 'He is going to be one of these guys.'
claims.passage: "He just gets what he wants," and "He is going to be one of these guys."
claims.inference: Verified in S09. This is Lind's characterisation to People in a June 2025 promotional interview, after recalling 'You'll get it, because you're you'. Only the reported behaviour (shortlist in confidence, naming rivals, C58) comes from the private call. Strongest evidence for the Three alternative, weighted accordingly.
claims.alternative: An affectionate prediction from a friend in press, one remove from People. Quoted and argued with, not omitted.

claims.claim: Producer Nina Jacobson said in the casting announcement, 'Jo prepared like crazy and stole our hearts.'
claims.passage: "Jo prepared like crazy and stole our hearts."
claims.inference: Independent corroboration from a decision-maker that his preparation was conspicuous enough to be the thing worth naming, which supports C11 from the other side of the table.
claims.alternative: Casting announcements are marketing copy designed to legitimise a newcomer, and 'prepared like crazy' is the standard way to justify choosing an unknown over known names. Corroborates that he prepared hard; establishes nothing about why.

claims.claim: Mckenna Grace said he kept the most intricate notes on Sunrise on the Reaping and that the two watched all the previous Hunger Games films taking notes, which led her to start journaling again.
claims.passage: "you kept the most intricate notes"
claims.inference: Third-party observation of diligence. The article no longer uses it against Type 9, since Nines can be diligent.
claims.alternative: Said inside a mutual-appreciation conversation in a fashion magazine, where both parties praise each other continuously. Corroborates thoroughness; carries no information about motive.

claims.claim: Julie Hosking, visiting the Invisible Boys set, found him remarkably upbeat for someone who had spent much of the previous week in tears.
claims.passage: Hosking found him "remarkably upbeat for someone who has spent much of the past week in tears."
claims.inference: The only substantial observed, non-self-reported behavioural datum in the packet, and it cuts both ways. It documents a real gap between his emotional workload and his presented affect, and it includes his own statement that the gap is habitual: 'I don't tend to wear my emotions on my sleeve like Charlie does... I have more access to my emotions, and I think that's been a very big gift.'
claims.alternative: A reporter's impression during a set visit is a thin behavioural sample, and an actor being cheerful between takes after crying on cue is close to universal, since the crying is work rather than distress. The durable part is his own statement about his habitual reserve, not the reporter's read.

claims.claim: He told Flaunt he is 'really happy, actually' and that 'You've just got to roll with it.'
claims.passage: He told Flaunt he is "really happy, actually," and said of industry pressure, "You've just got to roll with it."
claims.inference: Reopened 2026-09-13: 'You've just got to roll with it' is given as his attitude 'towards the pressures of the industry'. Recorded as disputed because it sits in tension with C12 to C16 and C23; the draft sets it out as the core of the Type 9 case.
claims.alternative: 'I'm chilling' as an answer to 'Who are you when you're not a character?' can be read as contentment or as deflection of a question he did not want to answer; nothing in the transcript settles which. The Flaunt characterisations are the writer's, not his.

claims.claim: He said in July 2025 that he wants to direct a film before he is 30 and has already started writing.
claims.passage: "I want to direct a film before I'm 30, that's my goal,"
claims.inference: Verified in S02 on 2026-09-13: 'I'm going to direct. That's the plan. I've already started writing. I want to direct a film before I'm 30, that's my goal.' The same interview mentions a film he and Hal were co-writing to star in; the draft-stage note that this was absent was an error (it is in S02, not S03). The article cites only the directing goal and 'I've already started writing'.
claims.alternative: Stated in July 2025 with no confirmed progress since; young actors routinely announce writing and directing intentions that do not materialise. He hedged it himself: 'I'm not saying I'll be good at it, but I want to try.'
claims.review_trigger: Before his 30th birthday (July 2035), or at any announced writing or directing credit, recheck whether the directing goal has advanced or lapsed and requalify the Type 3 paragraph.

claims.claim: He said of child actors, 'Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable.'
claims.passage: When Grace praised the young cast of _IT: Welcome to Derry_, he said: "Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable."
claims.inference: Verified in S03 with its prompt. In context he admires child performers' looseness as craft and then jokes about young actors outperforming adults. The article flags any meaning about himself as the author's open question, not his claim.
claims.alternative: A light craft remark; nothing is built on it.

claims.claim: As of September 2026, all seven episodes of East of Eden are scheduled for Netflix on October 1, 2026, and Sunrise on the Reaping is scheduled for US theaters on November 20, 2026.
claims.passage: all seven episodes of _East of Eden_ were scheduled for Netflix on October 1, 2026, and _Sunrise on the Reaping_ was scheduled for US theaters on November 20, 2026
claims.inference: US date reopened 2026-09-13 on the film's Wikipedia page (S21), which cites Lionsgate's own announcement; Variety Australia (S13) gives November 19, 2026 for Australian cinemas. Neither performance had been released as of the check.
claims.alternative: Release dates move. More importantly, the entire public estimate of him rests on unreleased work plus two 2025 streaming titles, so any framing of him as an established star is premature and will age badly.
claims.review_trigger: After October 1 and November 20, 2026, update to reflect actual release, reception and any date change; remove or rewrite any passage that treats the performances as unseen.

claims.claim: His released leads as of September 2026 are Invisible Boys, which premiered on Stan on February 13, 2025, and We Were Liars, released in June 2025.
claims.passage: As of September 2026, his released leads were _Invisible Boys_, which premiered on Stan on February 13, 2025, and _We Were Liars_, released in June 2025.
claims.inference: S06 states the Stan series 'premieres today (February 13)' in a piece dated 2025-02-13. S05 was published for We Were Liars' release on 2025-06-18 and S04 refers to its release day. Two released leads, both in 2025.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia is the only source enumerating the early credits, and its character name for Total Control ('Daniel') and other minor details are not corroborated elsewhere here. Keep early-credit detail minimal.
claims.review_trigger: Update the filmography after the October and November 2026 releases and at any subsequent casting announcement.

claims.claim: He told Fanning he wants to live in Los Angeles, New York or London even though his mother would rather he stayed home.
claims.passage: My mom doesn't really like that idea. She'd rather I just stay home. But I do really want to go live in L.A. or New York, or maybe London at some point.
claims.inference: Verified in S01. Used as one dated instance of holding his own plan against a close person's preference, relevant to the Nine alternative.
claims.alternative: Every young actor in this position discusses relocating, and a mother preferring a 21-year-old stay nearby is unremarkable. Useful as texture and as an unresolved fact, not as proof of anything.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck his stated base after the 2026 releases; if he relocates, update the passage and the mother's-preference framing.

claims.claim: He described the Haymitch casting call as coming while he was home with only his younger sister, and the two of them jumped up and down and cried together.
claims.passage: "I walked upstairs and we jumped up and down and cried together and I gave her a big hug."
claims.inference: Verified in S01 ('no one in the house besides my little sister'). The article sets this joy beside the 'more scared' answer so the win is not read as pure alarm.
claims.alternative: A warm anecdote told to a friendly interviewer; it evidences the scene he remembers, not a choice he made. Do not present it as him seeking family out.

claims.claim: Nearly all available evidence about him comes from promotional interviews given between February 2025 and August 2026, during the release or pre-release windows of four projects.
claims.passage: Almost every substantial source on Zada is an interview published between February 2025 and August 2026, inside the promotional windows of four projects.
claims.inference: Publication window of the record. The partial exception, stated in the next sentence (C88), is the Variety set interview given during the early-2024 Invisible Boys shoot. No biography, adversarial profile or long-term acquaintance account exists.
claims.alternative: None; this is a description of the source base rather than a contestable claim. Its consequence is that the type argument must rest on costly behaviour and cross-window consistency rather than on vocabulary, since humility, nervousness and gratitude are the default register of exactly these formats.
claims.review_trigger: If a substantial non-promotional profile, an adversarial interview or a post-release long-form piece appears after November 2026, revisit the type argument against it.

claims.claim: He told Variety Australia on the Invisible Boys set that he ended up being kicked out of school.
claims.passage: "I had a lot of stuff going on when I was younger and some schools just don't know how to handle that, and I ended up being kicked out."
claims.inference: First of his two accounts of leaving school, given on the early-2024 Invisible Boys set at 18 and published February 13, 2025. Paired with C07.
claims.alternative: Quote both accounts; do not settle which is true or build a causal claim on either.
claims.review_trigger: If the GQ Australia December 2025 interview becomes readable, or he gives a third account, reconcile with C07.

claims.claim: East of Eden began filming in New Zealand in October 2024 and wrapped in March 2025.
claims.passage: which began filming in New Zealand in October 2024 and wrapped in March 2025

type_hypothesis.against: Three things resist the reading. First, the most discordant testimony: Emily Alyn Lind reports him confiding the Haymitch shortlist and naming the big contenders during a private FaceTime (C58), and told People 'He just gets what he wants' (C26), which describes appetite rather than dread. Second, a run of his own statements describes someone settled rather than vigilant: 'really happy, actually', 'You've just got to roll with it', 'I'm chilling', a writer's 'uncommonly zen mentality' (C32, C69, C71), 'I feel like I can go toe to toe with anyone now' (C25), and a reporter finding him 'remarkably upbeat' after a week of crying scenes (C31). Third, and most seriously, the source base is structurally compromised (C44): apart from one early-2024 set interview (C88), every substantial source is promotional, and nervousness, gratitude and 'the cast became a family' are the house register of those formats. The record also lacks the most Six-specific markers: little testing of whether people can be trusted, no worst-case scanning beyond ordinary nerves, and no visible ambivalence toward authority.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: A Type 9 reading is genuinely strong. The accommodation language is mostly his own: 'You've just got to roll with it', blocking out noise, 'really happy, actually', and 'I'm chilling' as his answer to who he is offscreen (C32, C70, C71). He manages hard shoots through lightness and friendship, and he says he does not wear his emotions on his sleeve and that Invisible Boys gave him 'more access to my emotions' (C73), which a Nine reading takes as habitual distance from feeling; a reporter confirmed the placid exterior (C31). He also followed an instruction not to watch the 1955 East of Eden (C22). On this reading family trips are nesting, company is comfort, and the nerves are press idiom over an unruffled person. A weaker Type 3 case rests on Lind's 'He just gets what he wants' (C26, C58), the unbroken run of jobs (C09), the directing goal and early writing (C33, C102), self-crediting lines such as 'I can go toe to toe with anyone now' (C25), and a fear of how admired collaborators would perceive him (C13), which fits Three as well as Six.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: The types differ less in whether he is nervous than in what settles the nerves. A Six settles when trusted people and reliable structure are in place; a Three settles through visible performance; a Nine settles by smoothing things over or tuning pressure out. Zada's dated remedies repeatedly name specific people becoming dependable: 'once I step on set and meet everyone, I'll be fine' (C14, July 2025); the auditions as a way 'to meet all the people I was working with and feel comfortable' (C67, June 2025, relayed); confidence 'in the people around me' (C66); Glenn Close making it 'clear she was always there for me' (C19, July 2026); Pugh as daunting but someone who 'makes everyone feel so comfortable' (C94, June 2026); and, behaviourally, flying home to prepare the Haymitch tape with his brother and father (C11), though skill also explains that choice (C107). The fear of admired collaborators recurs across eleven months (C13, C93), after he said it had passed. Against the merging Nine specifically, he holds his own line: setting his own three-week deadline (C49), pressing the sound department to let him play music (C96), and planning to move abroad against his mother's preference (C40). The reaction to winning (C12, C48) is supporting evidence only, since a big obligation could also alarm a Nine or a Three and the same morning brought joy (C41). The reading would be weakened by evidence of him settling pressure mainly through performance and results, or of fame visibly settling him (C82).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Four things the reading does not account for. First, the appetite Lind describes (C26, C58), which a Six can have but which this reading does not predict. Second, leaving school: his two accounts assign the decision in opposite directions and the GQ primary is unreachable (C07, C45, S18); nothing is built on either. Third, 'Child actors are just so free, so loose. It's unattainable' (C36), a craft remark whose meaning for himself is the author's open question. Fourth, how he weighs a stated wish for privacy against how much he volunteers beyond promotional need (C24). A wing is not inferred.
